title: 🎯 Leadership Academy
theme: Develop your leadership skills through real-world challenges
description: You've been elected Class President with 500 Mento Coins budget! Lead your school through important decisions, manage diverse teams, navigate conflicts, and make choices that affect hundreds of students. Will you be a transformational leader who inspires change, or a servant leader who puts others first?

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Read each leadership scenario you face as the newly elected Class President
Choose how to respond -- each option reflects a different leadership style
Watch how your decisions affect Student Satisfaction, Team Morale, and Teacher Support
Manage your Student Budget wisely across multiple rounds of challenges
Complete projects and build your Leadership Influence to become the best leader possible
tips: Great leaders balance the needs of students, teachers, and their own team
Investing in Team Morale early makes later challenges easier to handle
Communication and Empathy scores unlock better options in later rounds

learning_objectives: Compare and apply different leadership styles including transformational, servant, democratic, and adaptive approaches to real-world school scenarios
Practice fair resource allocation under budget constraints, weighing competing priorities from athletics, arts, academics, and social activities
Develop conflict resolution and mediation skills by navigating team disagreements between council members with opposing viewpoints
Build emotional intelligence, empathy, and communication abilities essential for inspiring and managing diverse teams
Understand how leadership decisions ripple across stakeholder groups including students, teachers, and administration

rounds.title: Round 1: Defining Your Leadership Style
rounds.story:
Congratulations on being elected Class President!

Your first major decision: What kind of leader will you be?

Current status:
• Budget: {{mento_coins}} Mento Coins
• Student Satisfaction: {{student_satisfaction}}%
• Teacher Support: {{teacher_support}}%

Your leadership style will shape how you approach every challenge ahead.

Research shows different leadership styles work in different situations:
• **Transformational**: Inspire through vision and change
• **Servant**: Put others' needs first
• **Democratic**: Collaborative decision-making
• **Adaptive**: Flexible based on situation
rounds.setting: Student Council Meeting Room - First Day

choices.label: Transformational Leader
choices.description: Inspire through vision and big ideas. Challenge status quo, push for innovative changes. High risk, high reward. Students either love you or resist change.
choices.feedback: Transformational leadership chosen! You'll inspire through bold vision. Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela - leaders who changed the world by imagining better futures.

choices.label: Servant Leader
choices.description: Put students' needs first. Listen, empathize, support. Build trust through service. Slower but creates loyal following and strong culture.
choices.feedback: Servant leadership chosen! You'll lead by serving. Mahatma Gandhi, Mother Teresa - leaders who empowered others by lifting them up.

choices.label: Democratic Leader
choices.description: Collaborative decision-making. Seek input, build consensus, share power. Takes time but creates ownership and buy-in from everyone.
choices.feedback: Democratic leadership chosen! You'll lead through inclusion. Modern successful companies use this - everyone's voice matters, decisions are shared.

choices.label: Adaptive Leader
choices.description: Flexible approach based on situation. Sometimes directive, sometimes collaborative. Requires reading situations well. Complex but effective.
choices.feedback: Adaptive leadership chosen! You'll read situations and adjust. Modern military and business leaders use this - there's no one-size-fits-all approach to leadership.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant school auditorium filled with excited students, colorful banners hanging from the ceiling, a podium at the front, and students raising hands to share ideas, bright lighting creating an energetic atmosphere
rounds.coaching_moment: Consider how this choice affects your long-term resources, not just the immediate gain.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What tradeoff did this decision reveal? What did you gain, and what did you give up?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 2: Budget Allocation Crisis
rounds.story:
Your first major test! You have {{mento_coins}} Mento Coins for the entire semester.

Four groups are requesting funding:
• **Athletics**: 250 MC for new equipment
• **Arts**: 200 MC for theater production  
• **Academics**: 150 MC for STEM club competition
• **Social**: 180 MC for school dance

But you can only fully fund TWO initiatives. This decision will show your priorities and affect different student groups.

Current satisfaction: {{student_satisfaction}}%

How will you allocate resources?
rounds.goal: Make fair resource allocation with limited budget

choices.label: Equal Distribution (125 MC each)
choices.description: Split budget equally among all four. Everyone gets something but nobody gets enough. Fair but nobody's fully satisfied.
choices.feedback: Equal distribution chosen! All groups appreciate fairness even though budgets are tight. You avoided making enemies but didn't make strong allies either.

choices.label: Fund Top 2 Priorities (Athletics + Arts)
choices.description: Fully fund Athletics and Arts based on impact and need. STEM and Dance get nothing this semester. Clear priorities but some groups disappointed.
choices.feedback: Priority funding chosen! Athletics and Arts are thrilled. STEM and Social groups disappointed but you explained your reasoning. Tough decisions are part of leadership.

choices.label: Partial Funding + Fundraising Challenge
choices.description: Give each 100 MC seed money, challenge them to raise the rest themselves. Teaches entrepreneurship and reduces dependency.
choices.feedback: Creative solution! You're teaching self-reliance and entrepreneurship. Some initial grumbling but groups appreciate learning fundraising skills they'll use forever.

choices.label: Let Students Vote on Allocation
choices.description: Put it to democratic vote. Students decide priorities. You facilitate but don't impose your will. Builds buy-in but takes time.
choices.feedback: Democratic process! Students appreciate having voice in decision. Takes longer but creates ownership. Winner groups are grateful, loser groups can't blame you.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant school auditorium filled with colorful posters representing different clubs, students debating passionately around a large table, sunlight streaming through the windows, a sense of urgency in the air
rounds.coaching_moment: Think about trade-offs: what are you giving up to get this benefit?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 3: Team Conflict
rounds.story:
CRISIS! Your Vice President and Treasurer are in serious conflict.

The Issue:
• VP wants to spend {{mento_coins}} MC on big publicity event
• Treasurer says it's fiscally irresponsible
• Both threatening to quit if you side with the other
• Team morale: {{team_morale}}%
• Projects are stalling because they won't work together

The entire student council is watching how you handle this. Your team needs you to lead.

How do you resolve this conflict?
rounds.goal: Navigate team conflict without losing key members

choices.label: Support VP's Vision
choices.description: Approve the event, overrule Treasurer's concerns. Bold move, but risks losing Treasurer and setting bad financial precedent.
choices.feedback: VP is thrilled, but Treasurer submits resignation. You made a decision but at what cost? Sometimes supporting one person means losing another.

choices.label: Mediate Compromise Solution
choices.description: Facilitate discussion to find middle ground. Smaller event within budget. Takes time and skill but keeps both people.
choices.feedback: Mediation success! After 2-hour meeting, they agree on scaled-down event. Neither gets everything they want, but team stays together. This is leadership.

choices.label: Form Committee to Study Issue
choices.description: Buy time by creating committee to analyze both perspectives. Delays decision but reduces immediate tension. Risk: Looks like avoiding decision.
choices.feedback: Committee formed. Immediate crisis defused but both VP and Treasurer frustrated. You avoided the hard decision. Sometimes leaders must decide NOW.

choices.label: Redefine Roles & Responsibilities
choices.description: Address root cause: unclear authority. Create clear decision-making framework so this doesn't happen again. Transformational approach.
choices.feedback: Brilliant leadership! You recognized the structural problem. Created clear authority framework. Both VP and Treasurer appreciate clarity. You fixed the system, not just the symptom.

rounds.image_prompt: a tense student council meeting in a brightly lit school auditorium, members seated with worried expressions, two leaders standing at the podium, papers scattered, a sense of urgency in the air
rounds.coaching_moment: How might your team react to this decision? What about your customers?
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why did you choose this option? What were you trying to protect or grow?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 4: The Art of Delegation
rounds.story:
The annual Cultural Festival is approaching and there are five major committees to manage: Stage Setup, Food Stalls, Decorations, Entertainment, and Security.

You can't do everything yourself — you need to delegate.

Current status:
• Budget: {{mento_coins}} Mento Coins
• Team Morale: {{team_morale}}%
• Leadership Influence: {{leadership_influence}}%

Your council members each have different strengths:
• **Riya** — Creative and energetic, but can be disorganized
• **Arjun** — Detail-oriented and reliable, but struggles under pressure
• **Priya** — Natural leader, but sometimes bossy
• **Karan** — Great with people, but procrastinates

How do you assign responsibilities?
rounds.goal: Learn to delegate effectively by matching tasks to people's strengths
rounds.setting: Student Council Office - Festival Planning Meeting

choices.label: Match Tasks to Strengths
choices.description: Carefully assign each committee based on individual strengths — Riya on Entertainment, Arjun on Security, Priya on Stage Setup, Karan on Food Stalls. You oversee Decorations and coordinate everyone.
choices.feedback: Brilliant delegation! Each person thrived in their role. Riya's creative entertainment program was a hit, Arjun's security plan ran flawlessly. When you match tasks to strengths, the whole team wins.

choices.label: Divide Tasks Equally
choices.description: Give each person one committee randomly to be fair. Everyone gets equal responsibility regardless of their strengths or weaknesses.
choices.feedback: Fair on paper, but some struggled. Arjun was overwhelmed managing the chaotic Food Stalls, while Karan's Security plan had gaps. Equal isn't always equitable — fairness means giving people what they need to succeed.

choices.label: Handle Most Tasks Yourself
choices.description: Take on three committees yourself and split the remaining two between your most trusted members. You know you'll do it right.
choices.feedback: You burned out trying to manage three committees. The festival was decent but your team felt sidelined and untrusted. Micromanagement is the enemy of leadership — trust your team.

choices.label: Delegate with Mentoring Support
choices.description: Assign committees based on growth areas, not just strengths. Pair each person with a buddy from another committee. Invest extra time in check-ins and coaching.
choices.feedback: This took more time and budget, but the results were transformational. Arjun grew more confident under gentle pressure, Riya learned organization skills. You invested in people, not just tasks. That's servant leadership.

rounds.coaching_moment: Great leaders don't do everything themselves — they empower others to do their best work.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Did you prioritize efficiency or growth? What does that say about your leadership style?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Round 5: The Feedback Challenge
rounds.story:
Your Vice President, Meera, has been underperforming. She missed two deadlines, showed up late to meetings, and her committee's work quality has dropped.

Other council members are noticing and some are frustrated. But Meera is also going through a tough time at home — her parents are separating.

Current status:
• Team Morale: {{team_morale}}%
• Empathy: {{empathy}}%
• Communication: {{communication}}%

You need to address this, but how you deliver feedback will define your relationship and team culture.

How do you handle this?
rounds.goal: Practice giving constructive feedback with empathy

choices.label: Private, Empathetic Conversation
choices.description: Meet Meera privately. Start by asking how she's doing. Acknowledge her situation. Then gently share what you've noticed and ask how you can support her while maintaining standards.
choices.feedback: Meera broke down and thanked you for caring. She opened up about her struggles and together you created a plan — reduced responsibilities for two weeks with a gradual return. She became your most loyal ally. Empathy + honesty = trust.

choices.label: Direct Professional Feedback
choices.description: Be straightforward about the issues. Focus on behaviors and impact, not personal feelings. Set clear expectations and a timeline for improvement.
choices.feedback: Meera was hurt by the directness but understood. She improved her work but became distant. The team saw you as fair but cold. Sometimes being right isn't enough — how you say it matters as much as what you say.

choices.label: Avoid the Conversation
choices.description: She's going through a hard time — just redistribute her work quietly among other members. Don't confront her. Things will get better on their own.
choices.feedback: Other members resented carrying Meera's load without acknowledgment. Meera didn't even know there was a problem. Avoiding difficult conversations doesn't make problems disappear — it makes them grow.

choices.label: Address It in Team Meeting
choices.description: Bring it up in the next council meeting so everyone is on the same page. Transparency matters — the team deserves to know why things are slipping.
choices.feedback: Meera was humiliated in front of peers. She resigned from the council the next day. Other members lost trust in you — if you'd do that to the VP, would you do it to them? Public shaming is never leadership.

rounds.coaching_moment: The best feedback is specific, timely, and delivered with respect. Praise in public, correct in private.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How did you balance being honest with being kind? Is it possible to be both?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Round 6: The Great Divide
rounds.story:
A major conflict has erupted in the student body. The Sports Team wants the school's open ground allocated for daily cricket practice. The Drama Club wants the same space for rehearsals of their upcoming play.

Both groups have valid claims. The Sports Captain and Drama President are both on your council — and they're barely speaking to each other.

Current status:
• Student Satisfaction: {{student_satisfaction}}%
• Team Morale: {{team_morale}}%
• Communication: {{communication}}%

Students are choosing sides. Teachers want you to resolve it. The Principal says it's your call.

How do you handle this conflict?
rounds.goal: Navigate a complex conflict with multiple stakeholders
rounds.setting: School Assembly Hall - Emergency Council Session

choices.label: Mediate a Compromise
choices.description: Bring both sides together for a structured mediation. Let each group present their case. Facilitate a shared schedule — mornings for sports, evenings for drama. Invest in a portable stage to make it work.
choices.feedback: Both groups felt heard. The shared schedule wasn't perfect for either side, but both respected the process. The portable stage was a creative solution. True leaders find the third option when everyone sees only two.

choices.label: Side with the Bigger Group
choices.description: More students play sports than do drama. Give the Sports Team priority access and offer the Drama Club the indoor auditorium as an alternative.
choices.feedback: The Sports Team cheered, but the Drama Club felt dismissed. Several drama students quit. Majority rule isn't always fair — protecting minority voices is essential to good leadership. Democracy isn't just about numbers.

choices.label: Escalate to the Principal
choices.description: This is too divisive. Let the Principal make the call so you don't have to take sides. You'll implement whatever she decides.
choices.feedback: The Principal resolved it, but students lost faith in your leadership. 'What's the point of having a President if they can't make decisions?' someone said. Leaders who avoid hard calls get replaced by those who don't.

choices.label: Propose a Joint Event
choices.description: Turn the conflict into collaboration. Propose a Sports-Drama fusion event — an athletic performance showcase with dramatic storytelling. Both teams work together on something entirely new.
choices.feedback: A bold move! The Sports-Drama showcase became the highlight of the year. Both groups discovered unexpected common ground. Innovation often comes from combining things that seem incompatible. You created something nobody imagined.

rounds.coaching_moment: In every conflict, there's an opportunity to create something better than either side imagined alone.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Did you choose fairness, popularity, or innovation? What does that reveal about how you handle disagreements?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 7: The Trust Test
rounds.story:
A scandal hits the council. Someone leaked the exam schedule to students before the official announcement. The Principal suspects your council since you had early access.

After investigation, you discover it was your close friend and council member, Sahil. He shared it in a WhatsApp group "to help people prepare."

Current status:
• Leadership Influence: {{leadership_influence}}%
• Team Morale: {{team_morale}}%
• Empathy: {{empathy}}%

The Principal wants answers. Your team is watching. Sahil is begging you not to report him.

What do you do?
rounds.goal: Build and maintain trust through integrity under pressure

choices.label: Full Transparency
choices.description: Tell the Principal the truth about Sahil. Recommend a fair consequence — not expulsion, but a formal warning and removal from the council. Stand by your friend while holding him accountable.
choices.feedback: Sahil was hurt but eventually understood. The Principal gained deep respect for your integrity. Your team learned that trust means accountability applies to everyone — even friends. Real trust is built on honesty, not loyalty alone.

choices.label: Cover for Sahil
choices.description: Tell the Principal it was an accidental leak from the system. Protect your friend. Loyalty comes first — you'll deal with Sahil privately.
choices.feedback: The lie worked temporarily, but other council members who knew the truth lost respect for you. When the truth eventually surfaced, the Principal's trust was shattered. Cover-ups always cost more than honesty.

choices.label: Let the Council Decide
choices.description: Bring it to the full council for a vote. Present the facts neutrally and let the group determine consequences. Democratic accountability.
choices.feedback: The council appreciated being trusted with this decision. They voted for a fair consequence. Sahil accepted it better coming from peers. Shared decision-making builds shared ownership of values.

rounds.coaching_moment: Trust is earned in drops and lost in buckets. The hardest leadership moments define your character.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When loyalty and integrity conflict, which do you choose? Why?

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: Round 8: Leading Through Change
rounds.story:
Major news: The school administration announces a complete overhaul of the student activities program. Budget cuts mean:

• 40% reduction in club funding
• Two clubs must merge or shut down
• Sports tournaments reduced from 4 to 2 per year
• New mandatory community service requirement for all students

Students are angry and scared. Teachers are stressed. The administration says it's non-negotiable.

Current status:
• Budget: {{mento_coins}} Mento Coins
• Student Satisfaction: {{student_satisfaction}}%
• Leadership Influence: {{leadership_influence}}%
• Team Morale: {{team_morale}}%

As Class President, everyone is looking to you. How do you lead through this change?
rounds.goal: Lead a community through unwanted but necessary change

choices.label: Reframe as an Opportunity
choices.description: Address the school with a vision speech. Acknowledge the pain but reframe: fewer clubs means deeper ones, community service builds real skills, budget limits spark creativity. Launch a student innovation fund using the saved money.
choices.feedback: Your speech changed the mood. Students started brainstorming creative solutions. The innovation fund attracted ideas nobody expected. You didn't deny the difficulty — you channeled the energy into action. That's transformational leadership.

choices.label: Organize Student Protest
choices.description: Rally students against the administration's decision. Organize a peaceful petition drive and sit-in. Use your influence to push back. Students elected you to represent them, not to accept unfair decisions.
choices.feedback: The protest energized students but alienated administration. Budget cuts were slightly reduced but you lost teacher support. Sometimes fighting the system works, but the cost of confrontation is real. Pick your battles wisely.

choices.label: Accept and Comply Quietly
choices.description: The administration has decided. Fighting it wastes energy. Accept the changes gracefully, implement them efficiently, and focus on making the best of the new reality.
choices.feedback: Teachers appreciated your maturity, but students felt betrayed. 'You're supposed to fight for us!' they said. Compliance without advocacy isn't leadership — it's submission. Leaders must speak truth to power, even respectfully.

choices.label: Negotiate a Middle Ground
choices.description: Request a meeting with administration. Come prepared with data: student survey results, alternative cost-saving ideas, a phased implementation plan. Seek compromise while showing respect for their constraints.
choices.feedback: The administration was impressed by your preparation. They agreed to a phased rollout and kept one extra tournament. Both sides felt respected. Negotiation with data beats emotion every time. You proved that student leaders can be strategic partners.

rounds.coaching_moment: Change is inevitable. How you respond to it — with vision, courage, or fear — defines your leadership legacy.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When faced with change you can't control, do you fight, adapt, or lead? What's the difference?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

glossary_terms.definition: Leadership style that inspires followers to exceed their own self-interests for the good of the organization through vision, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration.
glossary_terms.example: Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech transformed civil rights movement by painting a compelling vision of equality.

glossary_terms.definition: Philosophy where the leader's main goal is to serve others. Focus on growth and well-being of people and communities. Leader serves first, then leads.
glossary_terms.example: Mahatma Gandhi led India's independence by serving people, living among them, understanding their struggles.

glossary_terms.definition: Ability to recognize, understand and manage your own emotions and the emotions of others. Critical for effective leadership.
glossary_terms.example: Great leaders sense team tension, understand different perspectives, and respond appropriately to emotional dynamics.

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now
